## 8. Models

### Neon glow (`lumenary:neon-glow`, models this process)

_From: Neon sign making; when: 1910s onward; works best on: Pictures with clear outlines, such as portraits and architecture._

A neon sign is a thin tube of gas that glows along its whole length, so what you see is a line with a soft halo. This treatment keeps only the edges of the picture and draws each as a tube. The glow comes from adding shrunk, smoothed copies of the line layer back at full size, which behaves like a wide halo around a hard core.

**How it is made, as the model does it:**

1. Blur the picture and find its edges with the Sobel pipeline.
2. Keep pixels whose edge strength is above a threshold set by the detail slider and colour them with a diagonal gradient between your two neons.
3. Shrink the line layer four times, each by half, and draw every smaller copy back at full size with additive blending.
4. Add a faint copy of the original underneath if you want it.
5. Flicker the whole sign with two sine waves of different frequency and an occasional dip to 45 percent.

**The maths:**

$$a=S_{\theta,\,2\theta}\big(\lvert\nabla L_b\rvert\big),\qquad\theta=\operatorname{lerp}(0.26,\,0.03,\ \text{detail})$$

_Line opacity: smoothstep of the edge strength of the blurred brightness L_b._ (primitives: edge-outline)

$$C_{\text{out}}=E+\sum_{j=1}^{4} g\,w_j\,\operatorname{up}(E_j),\qquad w=(0.95,0.85,0.75,0.65)$$

_Additive bloom: E is the sharp line layer, E_j the same layer at 1/2^j size, up() the smooth enlargement, g the glow slider._ (primitives: glow-bloom)

$$f(t)=0.93+0.05\sin(9.1\,t)+0.03\sin(23.7\,t)$$

_Flicker brightness; multiplied by 0.45 when (0.37 t) mod 1 > 0.965._ (primitives: flicker)

**Dials:** `detail` (Line detail) = 70 [0 to 100]; `glow` (Glow) = 75 [0 to 100]; `mode` (Colors) = "duo" (duo, source); `c1` (Neon one) = "#19e6ff"; `c2` (Neon two) = "#ff2fd0"; `base` (Show image) = 12 [0 to 100]; `flicker` (Flicker) = true.

**History:** Georges Claude showed neon lighting at the Paris Motor Show in 1910, and neon signs reached the United States in the early 1920s. Their colours dominated city nights for fifty years and still say “open late” to most of us. The glow trick used here is related to the mipmap pyramid, introduced by Lance Williams in 1983.
